**Authors:** Scott Coffin¹\* \[co-authors to complete\]¹ Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA), California Environmental Protection Agency, Sacramento, CA, USA\* Corresponding author: <scott.coffin@oehha.ca.gov>

_Intended for_ Environmental Science & Technology _(Article / Policy Analysis)._

## Abstract

Probabilistic ecological risk assessment (ERA) of microplastics rescales size-limited monitoring data to a common 1-5000 µm range and compares it against species sensitivity distribution (SSD)-derived thresholds. We conducted a fully two-dimensional (2D) probabilistic ERA for four central California rivers (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, San Lorenzo) and adjacent coastal water. Power-law particle size distribution slopes were estimated by maximum likelihood on individual particle lengths within a fixed 100–500 µm detection window. In simulations this estimator stayed unbiased when large particles were undercounted, whereas the cumulative-PSD regression of Segur et al. (2026) became too steep (Section 3.2). Exposure and hazard uncertainty were propagated through a Monte Carlo framework separating variability from uncertainty, with hazard thresholds derived from a probabilistic SSD (pSSD++) built on the ToMEx 2.0 database. At the field-standard 1 µm lower size floor, the food-dilution risk quotient (RQ) exceeds unity in both matrices (river median 2D RQ = 7.88, P(RQ>1) = 100%; ocean = 3.28, P(RQ>1) = 73.8%) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), whereas tissue translocation remains below threshold (river RQ = 0.194; ocean RQ = 0.037) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). This exceedance is **not robust**. It collapses below unity when the lower size floor is raised from 1 to 2.5 µm, and a formal decomposition shows it is generated by _which_ toxicity studies enter the SSD rather than by the extrapolation of exposure to unmeasured small particles: holding the study set fixed while rescaling exposure and hazard coherently leaves the river RQ at 0.636, and admitting sub-10 µm-tested studies collapses the food-dilution HC5 from ~1200 to ~68 particles/L to produce the exceedance. Because this ~68 particles/L HC5 reproduces the published field-standard value (Koelmans freshwater HC5 = 75.6 particles/L) [<sup>2</sup>](https://ftp.sccwrp.org/pub/download/DOCUMENTS/JournalArticles/1271_MicroplasticsRiskManagementFramework.pdf), the fragility is a property of the standard method, not of these sites. An independent two-segment (piecewise) exposure model, strongly favored by the data for river water, brings the river food-dilution RQ down to ~0.99 (ocean, where the two-segment preference is much weaker, falls only to ~1.39). We conclude that food-dilution threshold exceedance **cannot be excluded** but should not be reported as a robust finding of likely harm, and we offer the floor-sensitivity decomposition as a transferable diagnostic for microplastic ERA.

**Keywords:** microplastics; ecological risk assessment; species sensitivity distribution; particle size distribution; food dilution; probabilistic modeling; uncertainty

## Synopsis

A fully probabilistic microplastics risk assessment shows that the standard method's food-dilution exceedance is conditional on the assumed lower size floor and on mechanism-inconsistent toxicity-study inclusion, with implications for how the field derives and reports risk.

## 1\. Introduction

Microplastics are now ubiquitous in aquatic systems, and translating their measured occurrence into defensible ecological risk statements has become a central regulatory challenge. Two features of microplastics make this uniquely difficult. First, exposure is size-distributed across several orders of magnitude, yet monitoring quantifies particles only above a method-dependent lower size limit; in California and elsewhere, most microplastic surface-water monitoring data are based on particle sizes greater than 355 µm - the pore size of widely used manta trawl nets - even though toxicity is generally greater for smaller particles, and particles down to 1 µm are hypothesized to be exponentially more abundant than larger ones, so uncorrected monitoring data may not reflect true exposures [<sup>3</sup>](https://opc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Plastic-Strategy-Report-Public-Review-February-2026-508.pdf). Second, hazard is mechanism- and size-dependent, so a single concentration metric cannot capture toxicity across the size range.

The field-standard response, formalized by Koelmans et al. (2020), rescales measured concentrations to a default 1-5000 µm range using power-law correction factors and evaluates them against effect thresholds derived over the same 1-5000 µm range [<sup>4</sup>](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7547870/). Hazard is partitioned by two hypothesized mechanisms: food dilution, in which particles fill the gut and dilute nutritional intake, and tissue translocation, in which particles cross epithelial barriers and cause oxidative stress [<sup>5</sup>](https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/cjfas-2023-0023). These mechanisms are size-partitioned in a specific way - larger particles are more toxic at lower concentrations through food dilution (governed by ingestibility and gut volume), whereas smaller particles are more toxic at higher concentrations and are more likely to translocate [<sup>6</sup>](https://www.ecetoc.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/Current-research-initiatives-and-strategies-for-microplastic-management-in-California-Hampton-SCCWRP.pdf) - and are therefore aligned to different dose metrics: volume for food dilution and surface area for tissue translocation, rescaled to 1-5000 µm, with particles shorter than 83 µm most relevant to trigger translocation [<sup>7</sup>](https://microplastics.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s43591-022-00033-3). Applying this machinery, Mehinto et al. (2022) derived management thresholds for food dilution ranging from 0.3 to 34 particles/L and for tissue translocation from 60 to 4110 particles/L, adopting a freshwater food-dilution HC5 of 75.6 particles/L (95% CI 11-521) from Koelmans et al. and a marine HC5 of 33.3 particles/L from Everaert et al. [<sup>2</sup>](https://ftp.sccwrp.org/pub/download/DOCUMENTS/JournalArticles/1271_MicroplasticsRiskManagementFramework.pdf) The same framework has since been applied to the Laurentian Great Lakes [<sup>5</sup>](https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/cjfas-2023-0023) and to freshwater benthic ecosystems worldwide, where the conclusion was that risks cannot be excluded [<sup>8</sup>](https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/risk-assessment-of-microplastics-in-freshwater-benthic-ecosystems/).

Two coupled assumptions in this workflow are rarely tested. The rescaling extrapolates concentration far below the measurement floor, and its magnitude depends on the assumed lower bound. Simultaneously, the SSD's membership depends on that same bound, because studies conducted on very small particles become eligible as the floor is lowered - and small particles are disproportionately potent: HC5 estimates fall steeply with decreasing particle length, and fibers are roughly 100× more potent than spheres and fragments of the same length [<sup>9</sup>](https://microplastics.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s43591-023-00070-6). Whether the resulting risk signal reflects genuine exposure or an artifact of these coupled choices has not, to our knowledge, been disentangled on a real dataset.

Here we (i) conduct a fully probabilistic ERA for four central California rivers and adjacent coastal water; (ii) test the robustness of the resulting risk conclusion to the lower size floor; and (iii) introduce a decomposition that partitions the RQ's floor-dependence into exposure-extrapolation, hazard-alignment, and study-composition components. We use the new dataset as a demonstration case, but our central finding is methodological: the widely reported food-dilution exceedance is method-conditional in a way that has field-wide implications.

## 2\. Materials and Methods

The assessment is a fully reproducible R/Quarto workflow proceeding in five steps: (1) raw particle data to a power-law slope by maximum likelihood on a fixed detection window, with the cumulative-PSD (C-PSD) method of Segur et al. (2026) as a comparison and sensitivity; (2) probabilistic rescaling of monitoring concentrations by power-law integration with Monte Carlo slope-uncertainty propagation (Coffin et al. 2022); (3) an environmental exposure distribution (EED) by nonparametric bootstrap of corrected site concentrations; (4) hazard threshold distributions via probabilistic SSDs (pSSD++) using the PSSDplusplus R package and the ToMEx 2.0 database; and (5) risk characterization by Monte Carlo pairing of exposure and hazard, expressed as RQ = exposure/hazard and exceedance probability P(RQ>1) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

### 2.1 Study sites and monitoring data

Surface-water microplastics were characterized in four central California rivers - Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, and San Lorenzo [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) - and in adjacent coastal (ocean) water analyzed with the same µFTIR workflow as river water [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Monitoring concentration replicates comprised 217 subsurface and 253 surface river samples [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) and 85 ocean-water samples [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Per-river support was adequate for independent analysis: 221, 451, 161, and 374 particles and 106, 114, 119, and 131 monitoring replicates for Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, and San Lorenzo, respectively [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Sediment ("beach sand") was retained only as an illustrative methods demonstration and excluded from the headline risk conclusion, because its exposure concentration is a per-liter water value with no dry-mass basis rather than a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight measurement [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736); all results below concern surface water.

### 2.2 Particle characterization and detection floor

Particles retained from µFTIR imaging - after quality screening of the spectral match (confident library match, passing spectral-quality checks, and excluding non-plastic material classes such as mineral and organic matter) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) - were classified by shape (fiber vs. fragment, with fibers defined by aspect ratio ≥ 3) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Each particle's spectral-library material-class string was then mapped, by case-insensitive pattern matching, to one of thirteen polymer density groups (e.g., polyethylene, polypropylene, styrenic polymers, PTFE, polyester/PET, polycarbonate, polyurethane, polyamide/acrylamide, acrylic polymers, vinyl polymers, halogenated vinyl polymers, silicone polymers, cellulose derivatives), each carrying a literature density value taken from Hidalgo-Ruz et al. (2012) Table 2 [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Material-class strings matching none of these patterns retained the pipeline's legacy fixed default density of 1.10 g/cm³, previously applied uniformly to all particles [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The resulting per-particle densities were used to classify each particle's buoyancy as buoyant, settling, or neutral relative to freshwater (1.00 g/cm³) and marine (1.025 g/cm³) reference densities, feeding the vertical-transport diagnostics of Section 4.4 [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Only polypropylene and polyethylene were classified buoyant under both the freshwater and marine reference densities in this dataset, so "buoyant" was defined directly by these two polymer identities (PP + PE) rather than by selecting one of the two medium-specific buoyancy flags [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). We used these per-particle buoyancy assignments to test two hypotheses: whether ocean water is enriched in buoyant polymers relative to river water - which would support a surface-transport/retention explanation for the shallower ocean C-PSD slope (Section 3.2) rather than a source or fitting-window artifact - and whether river buoyant particles are relatively enriched at the surface versus the subsurface sampling stratum, consistent with local density-driven vertical sorting [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The full thirteen-group polymer × matrix composition was tested by chi-square, or by Fisher's exact test (10,000 simulated replicates) where any expected cell count fell below 5; the focused buoyant-vs-non-buoyant × matrix comparison used a 2×2 chi-square test with Yates' continuity correction; and the river surface-vs-subsurface comparison used a one-sided two-proportion test (H1: surface fraction > subsurface fraction), falling back to a one-sided Fisher's exact test under the same small-expected-cell rule [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Ocean water had no recorded depth stratum in this dataset and was analyzed as a single pooled group rather than assumed to be surface water [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). 

```{r ms-qc-values, include=FALSE}
qc <- P$particle_qc
wf <- qc$waterfall[["River water"]]
n_excl <- function(k) length(P$rescaling[[k]])
```

**Spectral QC and particle accounting.** Particle-level µFTIR records were kept if the spectral library match was rated confident and the match correlation exceeded 0.66; the bad-spectra flag in the instrument export marks correlations ≤ 0.66. Of `r format(wf[["Plastic (not mineral/organic)"]], big.mark = ",")` plastic-classified particle records from river samples, `r format(wf[["Spectral QC (confident, bad_spectra == FALSE)"]], big.mark = ",")` passed spectral quality control. The per-sample summary counted `r format(qc$summary_count_river, big.mark = ",")` particles; the summary counts are not a subset of the particle-level records (they differ by polymer class), consistent with separate upstream processing. Each sample's concentration was therefore rebuilt from its quality-controlled particle records, each record standing for the sample's aliquot extrapolation factor (extrapolated count divided by counted particles) within the analysed volume. Samples without particle-level records could not be rebuilt and were excluded rather than treated as non-detects (`r n_excl("river_excluded_no_particle_data")` river and `r n_excl("ocean_excluded_no_particle_data")` ocean samples). **\[FLAG – CONFIRM BEFORE PUBLICATION: the rebuilt-concentration basis assumes that the quality-controlled particle records, scaled by the summary's aliquot factor, represent each sample. This must be confirmed with the analytical laboratory, and the particle-level export must be updated for the 2025 samples.\]**

The µFTIR analysis used a ~4× objective with 25 µm pixel size, giving a practical minimum detectable particle size of ~50 µm (L_meas_min = 50 µm), a value already embedded in the correction-factor calculation [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736); particles at or above 100 µm are reliably detected by this system [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). We did not apply an additional magnification-based scaling: although Wang et al. (2026) report that a 4× µFTIR objective detects only 3 ± 3% of particles relative to a 25× reference [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), applying that ×33 factor on top of the existing correction factor would double-count the same particle pool that the power-law extrapolation already reconstructs [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

### 2.3 Power-law slope estimation and validation

**Estimator.** Each matrix's particle-size distribution was summarised by the differential power-law slope a of dN/dL = k·L^a. That slope sets both the correction factor used for rescaling (Section 2.4) and the particle-trait alignment used for the hazard thresholds (Section 2.5). We estimated it by maximum likelihood on the individual particle lengths, for a power law truncated at both ends of a window fixed in advance at `r P$meta$headline_length_window_um[1]`–`r P$meta$headline_length_window_um[2]` µm (doubly truncated Pareto; Aban et al. 2006). For L in [L₁, L₂), the density is f(L) = (1 − α)L^(−α)/(L₂^(1−α) − L₁^(1−α)) with α = −a; the estimate maximises the log-likelihood over α, and its standard error comes from the observed information. The window was set from detection, not fitted. The lower bound is where particles span at least four 25 µm pixels and µFTIR detection is reliable (Section 2.2). The upper bound is the 500 µm sieve boundary, above which large particles were undercounted (Section 3.2). Area and volume slopes, needed for hazard alignment, were estimated the same way over the area and volume windows implied by the length window, using each matrix's measured width:length and area:length² ratios. Per-river and per-coastal-location slopes used the same estimator and window.

**Why maximum likelihood, and why a fixed window.** When individual measurements are available, maximum likelihood is the most accurate and precise estimator of a power-law exponent. Least-squares fits to binned, log-transformed counts are biased and give unreliable uncertainties (White et al. 2008; Clauset et al. 2009). In simulation tests of eight size-spectrum methods, only maximum likelihood was consistently accurate with reliable confidence intervals (Edwards et al. 2017). When only binned data exist, the bins must be modelled explicitly (Virkar & Clauset 2014; Edwards et al. 2020). Regressing the cumulative binned distribution, the C-PSD method of Segur et al. (2026), comes close to maximum likelihood. Segur et al. developed C-PSD for binned literature data and validated it against maximum likelihood on raw particle data, which is also the method of Kooi et al. (2021). Two features of our data favour bounded maximum likelihood over C-PSD. First, Segur et al. note that the right-hand tail of a C-PSD slumps when large particles go uncounted, which steepens the fitted slope. Every cumulative point inside the fit window also counts the particles above it, so a deficit above the window biases the cumulative fit even after the slumped bins are removed. Second, the standard maximum-likelihood procedure with only a lower bound (xmin) is also biased when the upper tail is truncated (Deluca & Corral 2013). A window bounded at both ends and set independently of the data avoids both problems. We also tested a window selected from the data, which gave biased estimates even with complete detection (Section 3.2).

**C-PSD comparison and implementation check.** For comparison with Segur et al. (2026) and MPsizeBase, we also fitted C-PSDs with the Segur two-step LOD algorithm. Measurements were binned, cumulative and bin-normalised PSDs computed, and bins with positive residuals at or above the bin-normalised peak retained. All contiguous windows of ≥ 3 bins with R² ≥ 0.90 were then tested, the longest window selected, and log₁₀ N(≥L) regressed on log₁₀ L, with a = a_cpsd − 1. Our C-PSD implementation reproduced the Segur et al. reference PSD_fit.py code to machine precision for all nine matrix × shape PSDs \[**Table S2; Appendix B**\]. The C-PSD slopes are reported alongside the headline slopes (\[**Table 1; Table S7**\]) and were carried through the full exposure and risk calculation as a sensitivity (Section 2.7).

**Simulation test of the estimators.** To check estimator behaviour independently of our data, we drew particle lengths from a power law with a known differential slope (−2.4) between 50 and 5000 µm (2,500 particles per replicate). Three scenarios were simulated: complete detection; large particles undercounted (above 500 µm, kept with probability 0.4, as observed in three rivers); and small particles undercounted (detection rising linearly from 50% at 50 µm to complete at 100 µm). Four estimators were applied to each replicate: C-PSD, maximum likelihood above xmin (poweRlaw; Clauset et al. 2009), truncated maximum likelihood on the window selected by the Segur algorithm, and truncated maximum likelihood on the fixed 100–500 µm window.

**Heterogeneity among locations.** To test whether location-level slopes differ by more than sampling error, we applied Cochran's Q, inverse-variance-weighting each location's slope, with Q referred to χ² on k − 1 degrees of freedom and I² giving the share of variation attributable to true heterogeneity. Locations with fewer than 30 particles in the window were not fitted. As a check on the information-matrix standard errors, each river's particles were resampled and the slope refitted (particle-level bootstrap).

**Literature benchmarks.** We compared our slopes with Wang et al. (2026; µFTIR, Dutch river suspended solids), Segur et al. (2026; ocean and atmosphere reference slopes and the MPsizeBase compilation), Kooi et al. (2021; freshwater and marine defaults embedded in PSSDplusplus) and Zhao et al. (2026; 45-study net-trawl meta-analysis), each converted to the differential convention \[**Table S4**\]. Because MPsizeBase slopes are C-PSD fits, the like-for-like ocean comparison uses our C-PSD fits.

**Two-segment alternative.** Motivated by transport-filtering theory (Hoffman et al. 2026) and field evidence that single power laws can mis-extrapolate to small sizes (Thomas et al. 2024), we also fitted a two-segment model. The break point was chosen by AIC among the window's bin edges (≥ 3 bins per side). For rescaling under this model, the two segments were integrated separately, with continuity of dN/dL enforced at the break.

### 2.4 Exposure rescaling and EED

Concentrations were rescaled by power-law integration: for a differential PSD dN/dL = k·L^a, the concentration in \[L₁, L₂\] is proportional to k/(a+1)·(L₂^(a+1) − L₁^(a+1)), and the correction factor is CF = N(L_target_min, L_target_max) / N(L_meas_min, L_meas_max), implemented as correction_factor() following Coffin et al. (2022) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The convention is guarded by a rendered worked example: Koelmans et al. (2020) report that rescaling a 30-2000 µm range to 1-5000 µm at a differential slope α = 1.6 gives CF = 8.32 (100 → 832 particles/L) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), reproduced by the pipeline. The slope is treated as uncertain via a truncated-normal distribution, and following Hoffman et al. (2026), an explicit structural uncertainty of slope_structural_sd = 0.25 is added beyond the fit standard error, because transport can produce apparent dual-slope PSDs whose exponents differ by about two [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Corrected concentrations were bootstrapped to an EED at the 1-5000 µm target range.

### 2.5 Hazard: pSSD++ / ToMEx 2.0

Hazard thresholds were derived with the pSSD++ implementation from quality-screened ToMEx 2.0 records aligned to both ERMs using bioaccessibility models and particle traits, filtered to remove bacteria, plants, and HONEC endpoints and to pass minimum technical and risk QC criteria (43 unique species × polymer × shape combinations for freshwater) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), joined with a marine set of 493 records across 10 taxonomic groups [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Each endpoint was aligned by Monte Carlo simulation: for food dilution, a volumetric dose is computed from particle volume and organism gut volume; for tissue translocation, particle flux to tissue is computed with a size-dependent model that includes only particles below the 500 µm translocation threshold [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), generated over x1M = 1 µm to x2D = 5000 µm with an upper tissue truncation limit of 500 µm [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The resulting freshwater PNEC (HC5) distributions were median 68.5 particles/L (Q5 0.562, Q95 3570) for food dilution and 2960 particles/L for tissue translocation [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Figure S3; Table S3**\].

### 2.6 Risk characterization: MC1D and MC2D

Risk was characterized under two schemes. The one-dimensional (MC1D) scheme samples hazard and exposure jointly over 1000 draws [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The two-dimensional (MC2D) scheme, which is our primary basis, separates uncertainty from variability: the outer loop samples uncertain parameters (a correction-factor draw and one hazard draw per ERM/HCx; n_uncertainty = 300), while the inner loop samples exposure variability from the observed monitoring concentrations (n_variability = 1000) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Consequently each outer iteration is one plausible "world" of uncertainty, within which the inner loop yields P_exceed, RQ_p50, RQ_p95, and RQ_p99; the distribution of these summaries across outer iterations quantifies uncertainty in the risk metrics, while the inner loop represents variability in exposure [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). This distinction explains why MC1D and MC2D can share an RQ median while reporting different exceedance probabilities: MC1D reports a pooled/marginal exceedance, whereas MC2D reports the distribution (median and 5th-95th percentiles) of the conditional exceedance probability.

### 2.7 Robustness analyses

We tested three robustness questions. (a) _Floor sensitivity:_ the lower target floor L_tar_min was varied across {1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 20} µm and the full pipeline re-run at each. (b) _Decomposition:_ because moving the floor simultaneously re-extrapolates exposure, shifts the SSD alignment range, and changes SSD membership, we froze study membership at a common ≥10 µm reference set and re-ran the pipeline in scenarios isolating each component, attributing the RQ change in log space. (c) _Model-form bounding:_ the two-segment (piecewise) fit described in Section 2.3 was run as a labeled bounding sensitivity against the single-slope production model; a lognormal alternative was also examined for the sub-floor extrapolation (SI). (d) _Slope estimator:_ the full river exposure and risk calculation was rerun with the C-PSD slopes, each river's concentrations re-scoped to its own C-PSD window and each river's hazard re-derived with the same C-PSD slope draws (Section 3.2).

## 3\. Results

### 3.1 Particle characterization

Raw morphometry comprised 229 fibers (mean length 246 µm, range 75-2100 µm) and 978 fragments (mean length 98.9 µm, range 50-505 µm) in river water (n = 1207) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), and 117 particles in ocean water [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). River particles were dominated by polyester/PET (n = 300), polypropylene (n = 212), polyamide/acrylamide (n = 205), and styrenic polymers (n = 164) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Table S1**\]. Only 11 of 1207 river particles (0.9%) fell outside the thirteen matched polymer density groups and retained the fixed 1.10 g/cm³ fallback density [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

### 3.2 Particle size distributions and slope estimation

```{r ms-slope-values, include=FALSE}
fmt_a <- function(f) sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", f$a_diff, f$a_diff_SE)
br <- P$by_river
sm <- P$slope_methods
pr <- sm$per_river
sim <- sm$simulation
sim_b <- function(case, est) sim$mean_bias[sim$case == case & sim$estimator == est]
sens_risk <- sm$sensitivity$risk
rq_fd_hl <- sens_risk$RQ_p50[sens_risk$slopes == "Fixed-window MLE (headline)" & sens_risk$ERM == "Food Dilution"]
rq_fd_cp <- sens_risk$RQ_p50[sens_risk$slopes == "C-PSD (former production, sensitivity)" & sens_risk$ERM == "Food Dilution"]
rq_tt_hl <- sens_risk$RQ_p50[sens_risk$slopes == "Fixed-window MLE (headline)" & sens_risk$ERM == "Tissue Translocation"]
rq_tt_cp <- sens_risk$RQ_p50[sens_risk$slopes == "C-PSD (former production, sensitivity)" & sens_risk$ERM == "Tissue Translocation"]
def <- pr[pr$tail_ratio < 0.8, ]
het <- P$heterogeneity
w1 <- sm$sensitivity$W1_median_all
up <- sm$upper_500
rq_up <- function(rng, erm) up$risk$RQ_p50[up$risk$range == rng & up$risk$ERM == erm]
```

**Headline slopes.** With maximum likelihood on the fixed `r P$meta$headline_length_window_um[1]`–`r P$meta$headline_length_window_um[2]` µm window, the pooled river slope was a = `r fmt_a(P$pooled)` (n = `r format(P$pooled$n_window, big.mark = ",")` particles in the window). Fragments were steeper (`r fmt_a(P$fragment)`) than fibers (`r fmt_a(P$fiber)`). The ocean slope was `r fmt_a(P$ocean$all)` and the beach-sand slope `r fmt_a(P$sand$all)` \[**Table 1; Figure 1**\]. River slopes ranged from `r sprintf("%.2f", max(sapply(br, function(x) x$a_diff)))` (`r names(br)[which.max(sapply(br, function(x) x$a_diff))]`) to `r sprintf("%.2f", min(sapply(br, function(x) x$a_diff)))` (`r names(br)[which.min(sapply(br, function(x) x$a_diff))]`). They still differed by more than sampling error (Cochran's Q(`r het$df`) = `r sprintf("%.1f", het$Q)`, I² = `r sprintf("%.0f", het$i2)`%), though far less than the C-PSD slopes did. Consistent with fragmentation, fibers have shallower slopes than fragments; fine fibers may also be under-retained by a nominal 50 µm pore, making fiber concentrations a minimum estimate.

**The C-PSD slopes are steeper where large particles are undercounted.** For `r paste(def$river, collapse = ", ")`, the C-PSD slopes (`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", def$cpsd_segur), collapse = ", ")`) were `r sprintf("%.2f", min(def$cpsd_segur - def$tpl_mle_fixed) * -1)`–`r sprintf("%.2f", max(def$cpsd_segur - def$tpl_mle_fixed) * -1)` steeper than the headline slopes (`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", def$tpl_mle_fixed), collapse = ", ")`) \[**Figure 2; Table S7**\]. For San Lorenzo, whose C-PSD window ended well below 500 µm, the two estimators agreed (`r sprintf("%.2f", pr$cpsd_segur[pr$river == "San Lorenzo"])` vs `r sprintf("%.2f", pr$tpl_mle_fixed[pr$river == "San Lorenzo"])`). The difference traces to the upper tail. Above the C-PSD windows of the three steep rivers, which end at 480–535 µm, there were only `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(def$tail_ratio))`–`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(def$tail_ratio))`% as many particles as the headline power law predicts, against `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pr$tail_ratio[pr$river == "San Lorenzo"])`% for San Lorenzo \[**Figure 3**\]. This is the right-tail slump that Segur et al. (2026) describe. Maximum likelihood above xmin, the method behind the Kooi et al. (2021) and RIVM slopes, fits the same deficient tail and was even steeper (`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", def$mle_xmin_poweRlaw), collapse = ", ")`). Contamination did not explain the steep slopes: subtracting the expected field-blank particles from each river's size bins changed the C-PSD slopes by only `r sprintf("%+.2f", min(pr$cpsd_blank_subtracted - pr$cpsd_segur))` to `r sprintf("%+.2f", max(pr$cpsd_blank_subtracted - pr$cpsd_segur))`.

**Simulation.** With a known slope of −2.4, the fixed-window maximum-likelihood estimator was close to the truth in all three scenarios (mean bias `r sprintf("%+.2f", sim_b("complete detection", "Truncated MLE, 100–500 µm"))` with complete detection, `r sprintf("%+.2f", sim_b("large particles undercounted", "Truncated MLE, 100–500 µm"))` with large particles undercounted, `r sprintf("%+.2f", sim_b("small particles undercounted", "Truncated MLE, 100–500 µm"))` with small particles undercounted). The C-PSD fit became too steep when large particles were undercounted (`r sprintf("%+.2f", sim_b("large particles undercounted", "C-PSD (Segur)"))`), as did maximum likelihood above xmin (`r sprintf("%+.2f", sim_b("large particles undercounted", "MLE above xmin (poweRlaw)"))`). Maximum likelihood on the window chosen by the Segur algorithm was biased shallow even with complete detection (`r sprintf("%+.2f", sim_b("complete detection", "Truncated MLE, Segur window"))`), because that window is selected from the same data \[**Table S7c**\].

**Consequence for exposure and risk.** The estimator changes exposure and hazard in opposite directions. With the former C-PSD slopes, the river median 1–5000 µm concentration would have been `r format(signif(w1[["cpsd"]], 2), big.mark = ",")` particles L⁻¹, against `r format(signif(w1[["mle"]], 2), big.mark = ",")` with the headline slopes. But because each river's hazard is re-derived with the same slopes, the shallower headline slopes also raise the mean volume of the particles test species can ingest, which lowers the volume-aligned Food Dilution threshold in particles per litre. The river Food Dilution HC5 median risk quotient is therefore `r sprintf("%.1f", rq_fd_hl)` with the headline slopes, against `r sprintf("%.1f", rq_fd_cp)` with the C-PSD slopes (Tissue Translocation `r sprintf("%.2f", rq_tt_hl)` vs `r sprintf("%.2f", rq_tt_cp)`).

**Dependence on particles above 500 µm.** For a pure power law with the headline slopes, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(up$per_river$vol_share_gt500))`–`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(up$per_river$vol_share_gt500))`% of each river's 1–5000 µm particle volume would lie above 500 µm, the size range in which three rivers hold only about a third to a half of the particles the slope predicts; in the hazard, such particles count only for species able to ingest them (about half of the freshwater toxicity records). Setting the upper size limit at 500 µm for both exposure and hazard moved the river Food Dilution HC5 median risk quotient from `r sprintf("%.1f", rq_up("1–5000 µm (headline)", "Food Dilution"))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", rq_up("1–500 µm (sensitivity)", "Food Dilution"))`, and Tissue Translocation from `r sprintf("%.2f", rq_up("1–5000 µm (headline)", "Tissue Translocation"))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", rq_up("1–500 µm (sensitivity)", "Tissue Translocation"))` \[**Table S7d**\].

**Literature comparison and implementation check.** The headline river slopes lie close to the Dutch FTIR river slopes (median about −2.3; Quik et al. 2026) and within the range of Kooi et al.'s (2021) freshwater defaults, rather than at the steep end of the µFTIR literature where the C-PSD fits had placed three of the rivers \[**Figure S7; Table S4**\]. On the like-for-like C-PSD basis, our ocean slopes can be compared directly with MPsizeBase (Section 13.6 of the analysis report). Our C-PSD implementation reproduced the Segur et al. (2026) reference code to machine precision for all nine matrix × shape PSDs \[**Table S2; Appendix B**\].

![Headline power-law fits (fixed-window maximum likelihood) by matrix, shape and size metric; points are the cumulative binned counts.](../figures/cpsd_river_ocean_facet_plot.png){#fig-cpsd width="6.5in"}

![River power-law slopes by estimator. The C-PSD fit and maximum likelihood above xmin are steeper where large particles are undercounted.](../figures/slope_method_comparison.png){#fig-slope-methods width="6.5in"}

![Observed cumulative counts vs the power law with the headline slope, by river. Large particles are undercounted above the 500 µm sieve boundary in Carmel, Pajaro and Salinas.](../figures/slope_tail_deficit.png){#fig-tail width="6.5in"}

### 3.3 Polymer buoyancy and matrix composition

> **Editorial note (2026-10-15).** The exposure and risk numbers in the Abstract and Sections 3.4–3.11 were calculated before the spectral-QC fix, the particle-rebuild concentration basis and the switch to fixed-window MLE slopes. They must be refreshed from `data_output/psd_rescaling_params.json` after the production render. Sections 2.3 and 3.2 and the QC paragraph already read from that file.

Ocean water was enriched in buoyant polymers (polypropylene + polyethylene) relative to river water: 36.8% of ocean particles were buoyant (43/117, 95% CI 28.0-46.2%) versus 27.0% of river particles (326/1207, 95% CI 24.5-29.6%), a significant difference (χ² test with Yates' continuity correction, p = 0.033) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The full thirteen-group polymer × matrix composition test was not significant at that finer resolution (Fisher's exact test, simulated p = 0.085, minimum expected cell count 0.18) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), so the significant result is specific to the buoyant/non-buoyant grouping rather than the full composition table. Because the freshwater and marine buoyancy flags agreed for 100% of particles - no polymer group in the Hidalgo-Ruz et al. (2012) lookup falls within the narrow freshwater-seawater density band (1.00-1.025 g/cm³) - this enrichment does not depend on which reference density was used [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

Within river water, however, the buoyant fraction was numerically *higher* at the subsurface (31.6%, 160/507) than at the surface (23.7%, 166/700) - the opposite of the direction a local surface-accumulation mechanism would predict - and the one-sided test for surface enrichment was not significant (two-proportion test with continuity correction, p = 0.999) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Figure S6**\]. Local density-driven vertical sorting by buoyancy is therefore not supported within this river dataset, even though buoyant polymers are relatively enriched in ocean water as a whole.

### 3.4 Exposure

The median river rescaling factor was 22,465× (90% CI 3,106-175,514), converting concentrations measured over 165-385 µm to 1-5000 µm [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), and 3,834× (90% CI 655-23,195) for ocean water [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Bootstrap EEDs were 646.4 particles/L at the median (95th percentile 3,921.7) for river water [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) and 108.3 particles/L (95th percentile 184.1) for ocean water [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Table 2; Figure S2**\].

### 3.5 Hazard thresholds

Community HC5 thresholds at the 1 µm floor were 68.5 particles/L (food dilution) and 2960 particles/L (tissue translocation) for freshwater [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) and 24.8 particles/L (ocean food dilution) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The most sensitive species were Moina macrocopa (river food dilution, 9 species in the SSD), Ceriodaphnia dubia (river tissue translocation, 11 species), and Pseudechinus huttoni (ocean, 15-16 species) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Figure 2; Table S3**\].

### 3.6 Headline risk characterization (1 µm floor)

Food dilution is risk-dominant and tissue translocation is below threshold in both matrices. Under MC1D, river food-dilution median RQ = 9.03 (P(RQ>1) = 82.2%) and tissue translocation = 0.226 (29.8%) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), and ocean food-dilution RQ = 3.94 (91.9%) and tissue translocation = 0.039 (7.6%) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Under the primary MC2D framework, river food dilution = 7.88 (P(RQ>1) = 100%) and tissue translocation = 0.194 (20.1%); ocean food dilution = 3.28 (73.8%) and tissue translocation = 0.037 (7.8%) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Table 3; Figure 3**\]. Outer-loop uncertainty is large: the river food-dilution MC2D exceedance probability ranges from a 5th percentile of 0.076 to a median of 1.0 [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

### 3.7 By-river and individual-species screens

Exceedance tracked the fitted slope and correction factor across rivers, from Salinas (food-dilution RQ = 0.893, P = 0.475) and Carmel (2.876, 0.664) to San Lorenzo (11.694, 0.829) and Pajaro (68.150, 0.957) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Figure S4**\]. An individual-species early-warning screen - read as a companion to, not a substitute for, the community-HC5 RQ, following Thuy-Dung et al. (2026), who show an individual-species RCR > 1 can precede a community-HC5 signal by roughly a decade [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) - showed the most sensitive river species below threshold (Moina macrocopa food-dilution RCR = 0.173; Ceriodaphnia dubia translocation RCR = 0.004), whereas the ocean's most sensitive species Pseudechinus huttoni exceeded for food dilution (RCR = 4.151, P_exceed = 1) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Table 4**\].

### 3.8 The exceedance is not robust to the lower size floor

The food-dilution exceedance is a knife-edge on the size floor. Raising L_tar_min from 1 to 2.5 µm drops the river RQ below unity and it continues to fall: river median RQ (1D) = 9.403, 0.094, 0.053, 0.011, and 0.004 at 1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, and 10 µm; ocean = 4.058, 1.088, 0.070, 0.018, and 0.011 [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Figure 4; Table 5**\]. Counterintuitively, the HC5 jumps _upward_ as the floor rises off 1 µm: the river food-dilution HC5 median is 68.5 particles/L at a 1 µm floor but 1101.7 at 2.5 µm and 1319.4 at 10 µm [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). At the highest floors the marine SSD becomes data-limited - too few marine species remain to construct a food-dilution SSD at 20 µm, a genuine data-sparsity limit rather than a pipeline defect [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

### 3.9 Decomposition: study inclusion, not extrapolation, creates the exceedance

Decomposing the river collapse between 1 and 10 µm isolates three multiplicative components: exposure extrapolation contributes an 80.5× fold-change, hazard-alignment range 2.0×, and study composition 14.8× [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). By raw magnitude, exposure extrapolation is the larger lever - but it does not determine the exceedance. When exposure and hazard are rescaled coherently to the same range while the study set is held fixed, the river food-dilution RQ at a 1 µm floor is only 0.636 (1D), with the HC5 remaining high at ~1205 particles/L; allowing the study set to open collapses the HC5 and raises the RQ to 9.403 [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The exceedance is thus produced by admitting sub-10 µm-tested studies, which collapse the food-dilution HC5 from ~1200 to ~68 particles/L. This holds across risk statistics: under MC2D the fixed-study-set river RQ is 1.508 versus 12.383 when the set tracks the floor [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), an ~8× study-inclusion margin, and the ocean fixed-set RQ stays below 1 under both statistics \[**Figure 5; Table 6**\]. The tissue-translocation decomposition inherits a conservative caveat: the ≥10 µm composition freeze removes the small particles most relevant to translocation, so those diagnostics are a lower bound on translocation hazard, not a translocation risk estimate [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

### 3.10 The fragility is a property of the standard method

The food-dilution HC5 that generates the exceedance, ~68.5 particles/L for river water [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), reproduces the field-standard value: Koelmans et al. (2020) derived an ingestible-volume, bioavailability-corrected food-dilution HC5 of 75.6 #/L (95% CI 11-521) over the 1-5000 µm range [<sup>4</sup>](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7547870/), the value Mehinto et al. (2022) adopt as the freshwater food-dilution threshold [<sup>2</sup>](https://ftp.sccwrp.org/pub/download/DOCUMENTS/JournalArticles/1271_MicroplasticsRiskManagementFramework.pdf). Because an independently constructed SSD lands on essentially the same HC5, the exceedance is what the standard 1-5000 µm alignment yields wherever exposure is rescaled to that range - the same machinery behind the Great Lakes exceedances.

### 3.11 Model-form bounding: the two-segment exposure model

The data favor a two-segment PSD over a single slope, but the strength of that preference and its downstream effect on RQ differ sharply by matrix [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Table 6; Figure S5; Figure S10**\]. For river water, the two-segment fit places its break at 225 µm - within the measured 165-385 µm fit window - with a shallow fine-size slope (α_cpsd = −1.441) and a markedly steeper coarse-size slope (−2.166), and a ΔAIC of −44.0 strongly favors the two-segment model over the single slope [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736); the theoretical Hoffman et al. (2026) critical size (~36.2 µm) falls below this fit window, in the unconstrained 1 µm-to-LOD extrapolation zone rather than inside it [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). For ocean water the two-segment preference is much weaker: the break falls at 120 µm (within the 95-245 µm fit window), the fine- and coarse-size slopes are nearly parallel (−1.627 vs. −1.682), and the ΔAIC of −7.4 is roughly six-fold smaller in magnitude than river's, indicating far less evidence that a single ocean slope is misspecified; its critical size (~85.7 µm) likewise falls below the fit window.

Because the fine-size slope is shallower than the coarse-size slope in both matrices, the piecewise correction factor sits below the single-slope value in both, but the shrinkage tracks the strength of the break: for river water the correction factor falls from 22,465 (single-slope) to 2,403 (piecewise), a 9.3-fold reduction (piecewise/single ratio = 0.107), whereas for ocean water it falls only from 3,834 to 2,119, a 1.8-fold reduction (ratio = 0.553) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) \[**Figure S9**\]. This propagates directly to risk: river food-dilution RQ (1D, HC5) drops from 9.301 (single-slope; P(RQ>1) = 80.5%, 95% CI 0.13-2047) to 0.988 under the piecewise model (P(RQ>1) = 49.9%, 95% CI 0.01-218), while ocean food-dilution RQ drops more modestly from 4.421 (P(RQ>1) = 92.0%, 95% CI 0.54-119) to 1.394 (P(RQ>1) = 63.1%, 95% CI 0.22-32.1) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Tissue translocation remains far below threshold under both models in both matrices: river 0.261 (single) vs. 0.021 (piecewise), P(RQ>1) 30.9% vs. 10.2%; ocean 0.035 (single) vs. 0.013 (piecewise), P(RQ>1) 0.7% vs. 0.5% [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Sediment shows the same qualitative pattern - the strongest two-segment preference of the three matrices (ΔAIC = −70.9, break at 220 µm) and a comparable correction-factor reduction (ratio = 0.103) - but its RQ is not reported quantitatively here because its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value (Section 2.1) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

The direction of this sensitivity is not universal, however: independent field evidence suggests single power laws may _under_\-extrapolate small particles - in the St Louis Estuary a single power law extrapolated to 1.3-12 particles/L for 5-5000 µm while flow cytometry measured 600-1600 particles/L in the same system (Thomas et al. 2024), and Segur et al. (2026) find size-aligned 1-5000 µm concentrations average ~600× higher than single-slope extrapolated values [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The sub-floor zone is therefore unconstrained in both directions, and the piecewise result is a labeled bounding sensitivity, not a replacement for the single-slope production correction factor [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736).

## 4\. Discussion

### 4.1 What the numbers mean

Read at face value, the headline is that microplastics pose a likely food-dilution risk in these waters. The robustness analyses show this reading is unsafe. The exceedance depends on a single poorly constrained assumption - the 1 µm floor - and on a hazard-side step, admitting very small particles into a _volume_\-based food-dilution SSD, that is mechanistically questionable. The framework itself holds that food dilution is a large-particle, gut-volume mechanism and that small particles preferentially drive translocation, with translocation-relevant effects concentrated below 83 µm and aligned to surface area rather than volume [<sup>7</sup>](https://microplastics.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s43591-022-00033-3). Yet it is precisely the sub-10 µm studies - whose effects are more plausibly translocation- or oxidative-stress-mediated - that collapse the food-dilution HC5, consistent with the observation that chronic potency rises sharply as particle length decreases [<sup>9</sup>](https://microplastics.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s43591-023-00070-6). Their inclusion in a volume-aligned SSD may therefore mis-assign translocation-type potency to the food-dilution mechanism.

![Food-dilution RQ sensitivity to the lower size floor.](../figures/m12_floor_sensitivity_plot.png){#fig-floor-sensitivity width="6.5in"}

### 4.2 Can risk be claimed as "likely"?

We judge that it cannot, for food dilution as currently derived - but neither can it be dismissed. Against a robust claim: the exceedance evaporates by a 2.5 µm floor; a data-favored two-segment exposure model brings the river RQ to ~0.99, though the same model is only weakly favored for ocean water and leaves its RQ at ~1.39; it requires the contested study-inclusion step; the confidence intervals span orders of magnitude; and tissue translocation, the mechanism small particles actually favor, is below threshold throughout. In favor of caution: the small particles driving the signal are genuinely present and systematically undercounted near 50 µm, so exposure extrapolation is defensible and is in fact the larger raw lever, and field evidence indicates single power laws may under-extrapolate them (Thomas et al. 2024; Segur et al. 2026) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736); and under the field's own accepted HC5, the exceedance is real. The scientifically defensible register is therefore the one the field itself uses for microplastics - that risk **cannot be excluded** - rather than "likely," mirroring the benthic conclusion that risks to benthic communities cannot be excluded at current sediment concentrations worldwide [<sup>8</sup>](https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/risk-assessment-of-microplastics-in-freshwater-benthic-ecosystems/).

### 4.3 Contribution beyond a site-specific assessment

A fifth site-specific characterization would add little to a literature already spanning lakes, estuaries, and sediments. The contribution here is methodological and generalizable. (1) We provide a floor-sensitivity **decomposition** that partitions the RQ's dependence on the lower size floor into exposure-extrapolation, hazard-alignment, and study-composition components - a transferable diagnostic any size-rescaled SSD assessment can run to test whether its risk signal is robust or an artifact of coupled assumptions. (2) We demonstrate on real data that the food-dilution exceedance is study-inclusion-driven and reproduces the published field-standard HC5, elevating a local result into a structural observation about the method. (3) We implement a fully 2D probabilistic characterization, with slopes estimated by a bounded maximum-likelihood estimator that is robust to undercounting of large particles and a C-PSD implementation validated against the Segur et al. (2026) reference code, separating variability from uncertainty so the fragility is visible rather than hidden inside a point estimate.

### 4.4 The slope estimator is a first-order choice

```{r ms-disc-values, include=FALSE}
w1d <- P$slope_methods$sensitivity$W1_median_all
```

The power-law slope sets the size of the exposure correction and, through hazard alignment, the hazard threshold too. In this dataset the choice of estimator changed the river median rescaled concentration about `r sprintf("%.0f", w1d[["cpsd"]] / w1d[["mle"]])`-fold (Section 3.2), comparable to the floor-sensitivity and study-inclusion effects that are the focus of this paper. Three points guided our choice. First, when individual particle measurements exist, maximum likelihood is the most accurate and precise way to estimate a power-law exponent, and least-squares fits to binned counts are biased (White et al. 2008; Clauset et al. 2009; Edwards et al. 2017). The C-PSD method of Segur et al. (2026) was designed for the opposite situation, in which only binned literature data are available, and it should remain the method for comparing against MPsizeBase and other binned compilations. Second, every point of a cumulative distribution counts the particles above it, so a cumulative fit carries any shortfall of large particles into the fitted window. Segur et al. (2026) recognise this right-tail slump and exclude the slumped bins, but bins inside the window are still affected. In three of our four rivers, particles above about 500 µm were undercounted by half or more, which matches the 500 µm size-fraction boundary, and this alone accounts for the steep C-PSD slopes. Third, maximum likelihood is robust to such a shortfall only when the fit is bounded at both ends (Aban et al. 2006; Deluca & Corral 2013) and the bounds are fixed in advance. Choosing the window from the same data biased the estimate even with complete detection.

The slope also enters the hazard. Under the alignment rule, the Food Dilution threshold is computed with the same slope as the exposure, and a shallower slope raises the mean volume of the particles that test species can ingest. In our data the headline Food Dilution risk quotient was higher with the less steep maximum-likelihood slopes than with the C-PSD slopes, even though the extrapolated particle counts were about ten times lower (Section 3.2). The direction of the estimator's effect on risk therefore depends on the endpoint, and the slope must be propagated through both exposure and hazard before its consequence for risk can be judged. How far the Food Dilution result depends on predicted particles above 500 µm, where three rivers fall short of the power law, is tested by the upper-size sensitivity (Section 3.2).

We therefore recommend that assessments with particle-level data report a bounded maximum-likelihood slope with the window stated and justified from detection limits, alongside a C-PSD slope for comparison with the literature, and that they check the observed upper tail against the fitted power law before extrapolating. The fixed window has a cost: it uses fewer particles than a data-selected window, and it assumes that one power law describes the size range from 100 to 500 µm. The two-segment analysis (Section 3.11) and the structural slope uncertainty propagated in the Monte Carlo analysis (Section 2.4) address that assumption.

### 4.5 Food Dilution alignment: mouth sizes, volume slope and particle shape

```{r ms-fda-values, include=FALSE}
fda <- P$fd_alignment
cov_fw <- fda$mouth_coverage$Freshwater
cov_m <- fda$mouth_coverage$Marine
av <- fda$av_scan
fold01 <- function(env) { x <- av[av$env == env, ]; 10^(stats::coef(stats::lm(log10(hc5_median) ~ a_v, x))[2] / 10) }
sh <- fda$shape
sh_rq <- function(m, a) sh$`FD RQ median`[sh$Matrix == m & grepl(a, sh$Alignment)]
```

Three alignment inputs control the Food Dilution threshold, because the volume of ingestible particles is averaged from 1 µm up to each test species' mouth size, a range of about 11 orders of magnitude in volume.

*Mouth sizes.* Earlier versions of PSSDplusplus treated a missing mouth size as the 5000 µm upper limit, which assumes the organism can ingest 5 mm particles. Two of the most sensitive species in our SSDs were affected: *Moina macrocopa* (river) and larval *Pseudechinus huttoni* (ocean). The package now predicts mouth size from body length with the model of Jâms et al. (2020) and excludes records with neither value from the Food Dilution SSD. That excluded `r cov_fw$n_excluded_fd` freshwater and `r cov_m$n_excluded_fd` marine heterotroph records (`r length(cov_fw$species_excluded_fd)` and `r length(cov_m$species_excluded_fd)` species). Body lengths were used only for the life stage they were measured on. For five species (*Carassius auratus*, *Dreissena polymorpha*, *Hyalella azteca*, *Oncorhynchus mykiss*, *Oryzias latipes*), ToMEx gives body lengths only for other, mostly adult, life stages. Transferring those would overstate the mouth size of juveniles and larvae, so these records were excluded rather than imputed.

*Volume slope.* With package defaults otherwise, the Food Dilution HC5 changed about `r sprintf("%.1f", fold01("Freshwater"))`-fold (freshwater records) and `r sprintf("%.1f", fold01("Marine"))`-fold (marine records) per 0.1 change in the volume slope \[**Figure S11**\]. Our volume slopes are consistent with our length slopes for isometric particles, but shallower than the Kooi et al. (2021) defaults used in earlier assessments (Koelmans et al. 2023) and in the RIVM thresholds (Quik et al. 2026). This is the main reason our Food Dilution thresholds sit below the published values. It also means that site-specific alignment, which RIVM identified as a necessary next step, can move a threshold by orders of magnitude.

*Particle shape.* We aligned exposure and hazard with slopes fitted to all particles, fibers and fragments together. This follows every published application of the framework: Koelmans et al. (2020, 2023) used a single compartment slope; the package defaults are pooled-shape fits (Kooi et al. 2021); and RIVM did not separate shapes either (Quik et al. 2026). Fibers flatten our pooled slopes, especially in the ocean. Food dilution is a gut-filling mechanism, and fibers make up only about a tenth of the particles in the toxicity tests (Koelmans et al. 2023). So we also aligned both exposure and hazard with fragment-only slopes. This moved the Food Dilution median RQ from `r sprintf("%.2f", sh_rq("River (pooled slope)", "Pooled"))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", sh_rq("River (pooled slope)", "Fragment"))` for the river (pooled slope) and from `r sprintf("%.1f", sh_rq("Ocean", "Pooled"))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", sh_rq("Ocean", "Fragment"))` for the ocean \[**Table S7e**\]. We keep pooled alignment for the headline because it has precedent and matches how the reference thresholds were derived. But Food Dilution risk quotients, the ocean ones in particular, depend on these choices and should not be read as robust estimates of likely harm.

### 4.6 Additional structural uncertainties

Two further uncertainties bound the interpretation. First, transport can distort the observed PSD: size-dependent differential vertical transport (Hoffman et al. 2026) can produce apparent dual-slope PSDs whose exponents differ by about two [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736), affecting absolute concentrations through the correction-factor exponent and comparisons when shape, depth, or buoyancy classes are pooled. In this dataset the effect did not overturn the headline: depth-stratified fits were broadly consistent (subsurface a_psd = −2.875 vs surface −2.805, food-dilution RQ ≈ 4.8 and 4.2) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). Buoyancy gave a mixed picture (Section 3.3): local, within-river density-driven vertical sorting was not evident - the subsurface buoyant-polymer fraction (31.6%) was numerically higher, not lower, than the surface fraction (23.7%), the opposite of what surface accumulation would predict, and the one-sided test for surface enrichment was far from significant (p = 0.999) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736) - yet ocean water as a whole was significantly enriched in buoyant polymers relative to river water (36.8% vs 27.0%, p = 0.033) [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). These two results are not contradictory: they point to different spatial scales. A basin-scale sorting or retention process operating over the river-to-coast transition - plausibly relevant to why the ocean C-PSD slope is shallower than the river slope (Section 3.2) - is consistent with the data, whereas a local water-column stratification process within the river reaches sampled here is not. Second, fragmentation makes hazard time-dependent: as particles fragment into smaller, more bioaccessible sizes over time, HC5 values and risk ratios shift dynamically in accumulating compartments (Thuy-Dung et al. 2026), implying that the size-floor sensitivity documented here is also, implicitly, a temporal one.

### 4.7 Limitations

The µFTIR detection floor (~50 µm) means the sub-floor population is reconstructed, not measured, and the 50-100 µm class may be undercounted by 10-30% [<sup>1</sup>](file:11948#chars=529-736). The marine SSD is data-limited at larger floors, and the ocean fiber PSD is under-constrained. The correction-factor CIs span two to three orders of magnitude. Finally, the mechanism-misassignment argument is inferential: it follows from the framework's own size-mechanism logic and the steep length-potency relationship, but a definitive test would require re-deriving the food-dilution SSD with mechanism-consistent study inclusion (a direction we identify below).

## 5\. Environmental Implications

Microplastic risk assessments that rescale monitoring data to a common size range and compare it against SSD thresholds can produce food-dilution threshold exceedances that are conditional on the assumed lower size floor and on the inclusion of small-particle toxicity studies of contested mechanism. For central California surface waters, food-dilution exceedance cannot be excluded but is not a robust finding of likely harm, and tissue-translocation risk is consistently below threshold. Three implications follow. First, risk conclusions from size-rescaled SSDs should be accompanied by an explicit floor-sensitivity analysis, because the headline can invert across a defensible 1-2.5 µm change in a single assumption; the decomposition offered here makes that dependence auditable. Second, SSD construction should be mechanism-consistent - aligning sub-10 µm studies whose effects are plausibly translocation-mediated to a volume-based food-dilution SSD may over-state food-dilution hazard. Third, resolving the dominant uncertainty requires monitoring that resolves particles well below 50 µm, so that both the exposure extrapolation and the study-inclusion range are anchored in measurement rather than assumption. Until then, the most defensible statement is that microplastic risk to these communities cannot be excluded - a conclusion that supports precautionary monitoring and source control while the mechanistic basis of the thresholds is strengthened.
